input.command:
cd /Users/stayman/Personal/projects/my-hermes-agent
python3 - <<'PY'
p = 'workflow-system/product/arch.md'
s = open(p).read()
anchor = '## Open questions — deliberately NOT resolved here'
d21 = '''### D21 — Ingredient perishability orders the week; it does not select the dishes

**Decision (operator, 2026-08-23):** every recipe declares the shelf life of its most perishable key
ingredient, and `plan-week` uses it to **order** the week — short-shelf-life dishes early, long-shelf-life and
pantry-stable dishes later. It is **one factor among several**, balanced against D16's attended minutes, D20's
thaw and advance-prep constraints, preferences, and rankings. ⛔ **It is a tiebreaker on SEQUENCE, never a veto on
SELECTION.**

**Schema — two fields, added to the D15 frontmatter:**

```yaml
shelf_life_days: 3        # the MOST PERISHABLE key ingredient, in days from purchase
perishable_driver: fish   # WHICH ingredient sets that number — the audit trail
```

⚠️ **`shelf_life_days` is a MINIMUM over ingredients, not an average or a whole-dish estimate.** A dish of
fresh fish plus rice and soy sauce is a **2-day** dish, not a 30-day one: the plan must be driven by the
ingredient that spoils first, and averaging is what would silently schedule the fish on Friday.
📌 `perishable_driver` exists so a human reading the plan can see *why* a dish landed on Monday, and so a wrong
number is correctable at the recipe rather than being an unexplained ordering.

**Rationale:**

1. **It is the shopping trip that creates the constraint.** The household shops once and cooks across the week,
   so every ingredient's clock starts at the same moment. Perishability is therefore not a property of a dish in
   isolation — it is a property of **where in the week the dish sits relative to the shop**. That makes it
   inherently a *planning-order* input, and there is nowhere else in the design that owns week-ordering.
2. **⚠️ It must live in the INDEX, not only in the recipe files** — same trap as D20. `plan-week` reads only
   `00_Recipe_Index.md` (D15), so a perishability field present in `recipes/*.md` but absent from the index is
   **invisible at exactly the moment it is needed**, and the planner would order the week blind while the data
   sat one file away. Both fields are therefore index columns, and the index stays strictly derivable.
3. **Waste is the failure mode, and it is silent.** A plan that puts the fish on Friday does not error — it
   produces a spoiled ingredient, a substituted dinner, and no signal anywhere that the plan caused it. Unlike
   D20's thaw case (where the dish becomes *uncookable*, a loud failure), this one degrades quietly, which is
   precisely why it needs to be a scheduling input rather than left to the model's judgment per-turn.

**How it composes with the other factors — the balance is the requirement, not a nicety:**

| Interacts with | How |
|---|---|
| **D16** attended minutes | The morning window is the **hard** constraint; perishability is **soft**. ⛔ Never schedule a 20-attended-minute dish into the 6–7am slot because its fish is expiring — reorder the *other* days instead. |
| **D20** thaw / advance prep | A frozen protein has **no meaningful shelf-life pressure** until thawed. ⚠️ `thaw_required: true` dishes are the natural **late-week** candidates, and this is a genuine synergy: the freezer is what makes a long week work. |
| **Preferences** (`01_Preferences.md`) | ⛔ A hard-never is absolute and unaffected. Perishability never re-admits an excluded dish. |
| **Rankings** (`02_Dish_Rankings.md`) | Both are soft. A well-liked long-shelf-life dish may still take an early slot; ordering by spoilage is a nudge, not a sort key that overrides preference for the week's content. |
| **Weekend takeout** | Unaffected — a last-minute swap is normal (operator decision, 2026-08-22), so ⛔ never place a highly perishable dish on a weekend slot that may evaporate. **This is a real interaction:** the flexible slot is the *worst* home for the fastest-spoiling ingredient. |

⚠️ **Consequence accepted: `shelf_life_days` on a generated recipe is an estimate**, and produce varies by season
and store. It is marked the same way D16's minutes are (`# estimated, not yet cooked`) and corrected from real
experience — a spoiled ingredient is exactly the kind of feedback `meal-retrospect` can turn into a corrected
number. ℹ️ **Getting the ordering roughly right beats not modelling it**, which is the current state.

⛔ **Not in scope:** per-ingredient expiry tracking in `03_Inventory.md` with dated entries. That is a different
and much larger mechanism (it would need purchase dates per item, which only the receipt-OCR probe could supply);
this decision is deliberately the **cheap version** — one number per recipe, used for ordering. Revisit only if
the OCR probe (WP6) lands reliable purchase dates.

---

'''
assert anchor in s and 'D21' not in s
s = s.replace(anchor, d21 + anchor, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
print("D21 inserted")
PY

input.command:
cd /Users/stayman/Personal/projects/my-hermes-agent
python3 - <<'PY'
p='workflow-system/product/arch.md'; s=open(p).read()
start = s.index('### D21 — Ingredient perishability orders the week')
end   = s.index('## Open questions — deliberately NOT resolved here')
new = '''### D21 — Perishability is a property of INVENTORY, not of a recipe

**Decision (operator, 2026-08-23; ⚠️ reshaped the same day — see the correction note below):** perishability is
tracked on the **physical item in the fridge**, in `03_Inventory.md`, with a date. `plan-week` reads that inventory
and lets **use-it-or-lose-it pressure** pull dishes earlier in the week — and, when nothing can use an item in
time, says so plainly so it gets **eaten or discarded** rather than silently rotting. ⛔ Recipes carry **no**
shelf-life field.

⚠️⚠️ **CORRECTION — this decision first attached shelf life to the RECIPE, and that was wrong.** The
`shelf_life_days` / `perishable_driver` recipe fields drafted earlier on 2026-08-23 were **removed within hours**,
before any recipe was written. **Why it was wrong, and why the distinction is load-bearing:** a recipe-level number
is a *static property of a dish* — it says "this dish involves fish" — but the thing that creates urgency is **a
specific item with a clock already running**. Last week's half-bag of bok choy is urgent **because of when it was
bought**, not because of which dish it belongs to. A recipe field cannot express:
- *this* bok choy is 6 days old while a fresh one would be 1 day old — **same recipe, opposite urgency**;
- an item in the fridge that **no planned dish uses** (a recipe field is only consulted once a dish is already a
  candidate, so an orphaned vegetable is invisible to it);
- the **throw-it-away** outcome, which is not a property of any dish at all.
📌 **The general form of the error: I modelled the constraint on the artifact I happened to be building (recipes)
rather than on the artifact that actually carries the state (inventory).** ⛔ Nothing was built on the wrong
model — the correction landed before Phase 5 wrote a single recipe.

**Schema — `03_Inventory.md` gains a date and a shelf-life estimate per item:**

```markdown
| Item | Qty | Acquired | Est. shelf life | Use by | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bok choy 白菜 | 1 bag (~half used) | 2026-08-16 | 7 d | 2026-08-23 | ⚠️ overdue — use or discard |
| Salmon fillet | 2 pieces | 2026-08-22 | 2 d (fresh) / 90 d (frozen) | 2026-08-24 | in freezer |
| Soy sauce | 1 bottle | 2026-06-01 | pantry | — | |
```

- **`Acquired`** is the clock's start. ⚠️ It is the field the whole mechanism rests on, and it is the one a
  receipt actually supplies — which is why WP6's OCR probe matters here beyond item names.
- **`Use by`** is **derived** (`Acquired` + shelf life), not independently authored. ⛔ On disagreement the
  derivation wins, the same discipline as D15's index.
- **`pantry`** is a legal shelf-life value meaning *no meaningful clock* — rice, soy sauce, frozen goods. It keeps
  the column total rather than making staples look like an omission.
- ⚠️ **A frozen item's clock is the FROZEN one** until it is thawed. This is where D20 meets D21: `thaw_required`
  dishes draw on items with **no urgency**, which is exactly what makes the freezer the tool for late in the week.

**How `plan-week` uses it — pressure, not a veto:**

1. **Read the inventory first, and compute what is expiring inside the plan's horizon.** Items past or near
   `Use by` become **use-it-or-lose-it candidates**.
2. **Prefer dishes that consume those items, and place them EARLY.** This is the operator's requirement stated
   directly: things that expire quickly get cooked in the first half of the week.
3. ⛔ **When nothing fits, say so.** If an expiring item has no dish that can use it in time — or using it would
   violate a hard-never, blow the 6–7am attended-minutes budget, or break the no-reheat rule — the plan states
   the item and recommends **eat-it-standalone or discard**. ⚠️ **This is a required output, not a fallback:** a
   plan that silently omits a rotting vegetable has failed at the one thing this decision exists for.
4. **Shopping list subtraction.** An item already in the fridge and still good must **not** be re-bought — the
   inventory is consulted before the list is emitted, which is the same read serving two purposes.

**Why not on the recipe (the balance this preserves):** perishability enters planning as a **weight on
sequence**, alongside D16's attended minutes, D20's thaw/advance-prep, preferences, and rankings. Keeping it on
inventory means it is **evaluated fresh at every planning turn against real dates**, rather than baked into a
dish's identity. ⛔ It still never overrides a hard-never and never overrides the morning attended-minutes budget
— reorder the *other* days instead.

⚠️ **Consequence accepted: this depends on the inventory being reasonably current**, which depends on
`receipt-intake` and on the cooking-confirmation decrement (WBS 4.6). A stale inventory produces stale urgency —
⛔ **so the dates must be shown to the household in the plan, never used silently.** A wrong `Acquired` date the
household can see is correctable; one that only the model consults is not. ℹ️ Shelf-life estimates start as
generic per-ingredient defaults and are corrected from experience, the same way D16's minutes are.

⛔ **Not in scope:** per-item barcode/lot tracking, or inferring what was consumed without being told. The
cooking-confirmation path (4.6) already owns decrement, including its partial-consumption semantics.

---

'''

open(p,'w').write(s)
print("D21 rewritten as inventory-based")

## SURFACE-2026-08-23-CONSTRAINT-MODELLED-ON-THE-ARTIFACT-IN-HAND
- **Source:** feature:build (M9/WP3 Phase 1)
- **Target level:** product:arch
- **Type:** gap
- **Summary:** Asked to make meal planning account for **ingredient freshness**, I modelled it as a **recipe**
  field (`shelf_life_days` / `perishable_driver`) — because recipes were the artifact I was already building.
  The operator corrected it within the hour: perishability belongs to the **inventory item** in the fridge
  (*"if there's some vegi left from last week, it should be either cooked quickly or just throw away"*).
  Recorded as `arch.md` **D21**; nothing was built on the wrong model.
- **Context:** ⚠️ **The wrong model was not obviously wrong** — it satisfied the literal request ("plan
  fast-spoiling things early"), it typechecked against the existing D15/D16/D20 schema, and it produced a
  coherent decision document with a rationale, a composition table, and verification outcomes. **Three things it
  structurally could not do**, none of which surfaced from reasoning about the schema: (1) a recipe field is a
  static property of a *dish*, so *this* 6-day-old bok choy and a fresh one are **indistinguishable — same
  recipe, opposite urgency**; (2) it is only consulted once a dish is already a candidate, so an item **no
  planned dish uses** is invisible; (3) it has no way to express **throw it away**, which is not a property of
  any dish. 📌 **The general form: I attached the constraint to the artifact in my hands rather than to the
  artifact that carries the state.** ⚠️ This is a *design*-time analogue of the guard-discipline rule about
  deriving the subject set — same failure (wrong subject), different phase, and no injection or test could have
  caught it because the model was internally consistent. ℹ️ The tell available at the time: the decision needed a
  clause ruling **dated inventory entries out of scope** — i.e. it was actively fencing off the mechanism it
  actually needed. **A decision that must exclude the obvious solution to its own problem is a signal to
  re-examine the model, not a scope boundary to document.**
- **Suggested action:** When a new factor arrives mid-build, ask **"which artifact owns this state, and does it
  have a clock?"** before extending whatever schema is already open. ⚠️ Worth a look at whether the other M9
  decisions attach state to the right artifact — D17's rankings and D13's household facts are the candidates,
  since both were also written while a different artifact was in hand.
- **Priority:** low — the instance is corrected before any build; the value is the tell (a self-excluding scope
  clause) and the question, both cheap to apply.
- **Status:** open
EOF

My commit touched **no** code, tests, or config — only docs and the plan. Combined with the `bin/deploy --dry-run` exit 1 I measured *before* editing anything, the 5 failures are conclusively pre-existing and caused by the box-side allowlist divergence.

Phase 1 is complete and verified. Here's where things stand.

## Phase 1 delivered

**`docs/mimi-ingredient-bootstrap-checklist.md`** — the elicitation instrument. Six categories, four marking columns, two tiers. Measured: **80 ingredient rows, 320 marking cells, 316 blank, exactly 4 marked** — your two stated facts and nothing else. The pre-K nut/reheat item is recorded as a **question**, not a rule. All 10 planned observable outcomes pass.

## Your freshness requirement — and my wrong first pass

You were right to correct me. I attached shelf life to the **recipe**, and that model structurally cannot do the job:

- *this* 6-day-old bok choy and a fresh one are the **same recipe, opposite urgency**
- an item **no planned dish uses** is invisible to a recipe field
- it has no way to say **throw it away** — that isn't a property of any dish

Now `arch.md` **D21**: `03_Inventory.md` carries `Acquired` · `Est. shelf life` (`pantry` = no clock) · derived `Use by`. `plan-week` reads inventory **first**, pulls dishes consuming expiring items **early**, treats frozen/`thaw_required` as late-week — and **must say so** when nothing can use an item in time, recommending eat-or-discard. It never overrides a hard-never or the 6–7am attended-minutes budget; it reorders the other days instead. Nothing was built on the wrong model — Phase 5 hadn't written a recipe yet, and it now carries a negative assertion so the wrong model can't creep back.

The tell I missed at the time: the wrong version needed a clause ruling dated inventory entries *out of scope* — it was fencing off the very mechanism it needed.

## One thing needs your decision before Phase 2

**Noey's box config has `command_allowlist: ['execute_code']`, and no repo config has it.** Upstream confirms this is written when someone picks **"allow permanently"** at an approval prompt — so it's a real choice made in chat, not drift.

Consequences: `bin/deploy` refuses every run, which blocks Phase 2 onward, and it fails 5 hermetic tests (**492 passed / 5 failed**, exit 0 — all 5 in the two blocks that shell out to deploy; my commit touched no code, and deploy was already refusing before I edited anything).

⛔ I have **not** run `--force-config`, because that would destroy the setting — the same class of revert that already happened once in WP6. Two reassurances I did measure: the box's 02:03 rewrite **lost zero keys** (111 → 113, the additions being our own D11/D12), and the 28 KB → 7.4 KB shrink is just Hermes dropping our comments.

**Did you intend to permanently approve `execute_code` for Noey?** If yes, I'll adopt it into `profiles/noey/config.yaml` with a comment and deploy — the gate and all 5 tests clear. It's a standing grant of code execution, so I'd rather have your explicit yes than transcribe it silently.

Also worth knowing: the hermetic suite now takes **~430s**, double the registry's ~210s — likely those 5 failing deploy paths each paying a full round-trip to the box. Registry updated with a note not to average the two readings.

:::tip
Run `/usage` periodically to see your token consumption. Run `/insights` for a broader view of usage patterns over the last 30 days.
:::

## Messaging Tips

### Set a Home Channel

Use `/sethome` in your preferred Telegram or Discord chat to designate it as the home channel. Cron job results and scheduled task outputs are delivered here. Without it, the agent has nowhere to send proactive messages.

### Use /title to Organize Sessions

Name your sessions with `/title auth-refactor` or `/title research-llm-quantization`. Named sessions are easy to find with `hermes sessions list` and resume with `hermes -r "auth-refactor"`. Unnamed sessions pile up and become impossible to distinguish.

### DM Pairing for Team Access

Instead of manually collecting user IDs for allowlists, enable DM pairing. When a teammate DMs the bot, they get a one-time pairing code. You approve it with `hermes pairing approve telegram XKGH5N7P` — simple and secure.

### Tool Progress Display Modes

Use `/verbose` to control how much tool activity you see. In messaging platforms, less is usually more — keep it on "new" to see just new tool calls. In the CLI, "all" gives you a satisfying live view of everything the agent does.

Once upstream is healthy, `/platform resume <name>` clears the breaker and re-arms the adapter.

### Restart notifications

When the gateway restarts (or is shut down with in-flight sessions), it can send a one-shot "the agent is back" / "the agent was interrupted" message to each platform's home channel. This is controlled per-platform by the `gateway_restart_notification` flag in `gateway-config.yaml`, which defaults to `true`:

```yaml
gateway:
  platforms:
    telegram:
      home_chat_id: "123456789"
      gateway_restart_notification: false   # opt out for this platform
    discord:
      home_chat_id: "987654321"
      # gateway_restart_notification omitted → defaults to true
```

    slack:

def persist_home_channel(home: HomeChannel, *, enabled_if_new: bool = False) -> None:
    """Persist a logical home without falsely enabling a Relay-fronted adapter."""
    from hermes_cli.config import load_config, save_config

    config = load_config()
    platforms = config.setdefault("platforms", {})
    if not isinstance(platforms, dict):
        platforms = {}
        config["platforms"] = platforms
    platform_config = platforms.setdefault(home.platform.value, {})
    if not isinstance(platform_config, dict):
        platform_config = {}
        platforms[home.platform.value] = platform_config
    if enabled_if_new:
        platform_config.setdefault("enabled", True)
    platform_config["home_channel"] = home.to_dict()
    save_config(config)

    via the `session_reset` section in config.yaml (or gateway.json

I have both group IDs. Now, one important consideration before I write anything.

The `home_channel` is where **cron results and proactive messages** get delivered. Both agents are **pull-only by design** (D6a; M9 operator decision 1) — so nothing will ever actually be delivered there. The shared group is the right choice for both: it's where each agent's work is jointly visible, and it's already allowlisted.

cat >> docs/lessons/guard-discipline.md <<'EOF'

---

## A guard that is FIXED can un-cover a neighbour — the second-order cost of a derived exemption

**Measured 2026-08-23 (M9/WP3), two profiles at once.**

The suite forbids comment prose inside any `sed`-extracted top-level key range, and exempts exactly one
key: **the last one**, whose range runs to EOF and therefore legitimately holds upstream's ~50-line
trailing commentary. That exemption used to be spelled by name (`_config_version`) with a written warning
that adding a key after it would break the assumption. M5/WP6 did exactly that, the warning did not fire,
and the exemption was rewritten to be **derived** — whichever key appears last is exempt. ✅ **That fix
was correct and it worked.**

Then two new top-level keys were appended, and the suite went red — on **`_config_version`** and
**`gateway`**, keys whose comment blocks *nobody had touched*.

📌 **THE MECHANISM: moving an exemption ONTO a new key moves it OFF an old one.** The derived exemption
tracked the new last key exactly as designed; what nothing had recorded is that the **displaced** key
inherits whatever content sits in its range — here, upstream's commentary, which our diff never mentions.
⛔ **So the diagnostic names the victim, not the cause.** An author reading *"comment prose sits inside the
sed range of: gateway"* looks at `gateway:`, finds a two-line block they did not write, and has no path
from there to *"you appended a key at EOF."*

⚠️ **This is NOT the M5/WP6 defect recurring.** That one was an exemption failing to move. This one is an
exemption moving *correctly* and stranding its previous holder. **A derived subject set fixed the first
and created the second** — the two are opposite failure modes of the same mechanism, and the fix for one
is what enables the other.

### Relocating made it worse twice before it made it better

Three reorderings, each producing a **different single offender**:

| Attempt | Placement | Offender |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `platforms:` appended at EOF | `_config_version` (both profiles) |
| 2 | `platforms:` moved above `_config_version` | `_config_version` (noey) / **`gateway`** (mimi) |
| 3 | every top-level key moved **above** the commentary banner | **none** |

⛔ A textbook run of *relocating a defect is not fixing it* — attempt 2 moved the failure to a **new key on
one profile only**, which reads as progress and is not. The invariant that finally held is **positional and
must be stated as such**: *every top-level key must appear BEFORE upstream's trailing commentary block; only
the key immediately preceding it may be last.*

📌 **THE TRANSFERABLE RULE: when a guard's exemption is derived from position, adding an element at that
position is a coverage change, not just an addition.** Before appending, ask *which element currently holds
the exemption, and what is in its range once it stops holding it?* ⚠️ And when a guard fails naming a
subject you never edited, **suspect the exemption boundary before suspecting the named subject** — the
named key is where the consequence landed, not where the change was made.

ℹ️ Related but distinct from the `head -1` rule above (*a derived set consumed one element at a time*).
There, coverage shrank because the loop ignored most of the set. Here the loop consumed **all** of it
correctly, and coverage moved because the **exemption** did. Deriving the subject set does not make the
*exemption* self-maintaining.
EOF

Let me wait for the monitor rather than keep polling — I'll summarize where things stand.

Here's the state of play, including a correction to something I told you earlier.

## Correction: I called the fix confirmed too early

I told you "the fix is working" based on **0 failures at line 123** of a 603-line run. That was a partial read presented as a result. The actual outcome was **495 passed / 2 failed** — better than the 5 I started with, but not clean, and I'd already reported it as such.

The 2 failures were **mine**, and a real guard caught a real defect I introduced.

## What went wrong, and it's an interesting one

The suite forbids comment prose inside any `sed`-extracted config key range, exempting only the **last** top-level key — whose range runs to EOF and legitimately holds ~50 lines of upstream's own commentary.

By appending `platforms:` and `command_allowlist:` at end-of-file, I **moved that exemption onto my new keys and off the old holders** — which then owned commentary *they never authored*. The suite went red naming `gateway` and `_config_version`, keys whose own contents were correct and untouched.

Two things worth noting:

- **The diagnostic names the victim, not the cause.** Reading "comment prose sits inside the sed range of: `gateway`" sends you to inspect a two-line block that is perfectly fine, forty lines from the actual change.
- **This is the mirror image of a defect that guard was already fixed for.** M5/WP6 hit an exemption that failed to *move*; the fix made it derived. Mine is that same exemption moving *correctly* and stranding its predecessor. The fix for the first failure mode is what enables the second.

It took **three** placements to land: append at EOF → `_config_version` offends; move above it → the failure jumps to `gateway` on *one* profile only (which reads as progress and isn't); move every key above the commentary banner → clean. A textbook run of *relocating a defect is not fixing it*.

## Current state

- **Both profiles: zero offenders** under the guard's exact logic, re-derived rather than spot-checked.
- **Semantically identical** to the behaviorally-verified commit — 116/113 leaf keys, **zero lost, added, or changed**. Comments and ordering only.

Raised to medium, actionable at the M9 close.

range, exempting exactly one key: the LAST one, whose range runs to EOF and so
legitimately holds upstream's ~50-line trailing commentary. That exemption is

never edited.

move; this is one moving correctly and stranding its predecessor. The fix for
the first failure mode is what enables the second.

Relocating made it worse twice before better -- three placements, three
different offender sets:

  3. all keys above the upstream commentary banner -> none

progress and is not: a textbook run of "relocating a defect is not fixing it."

the commentary block; only the key immediately preceding it may be last.

# 米米小厨 / Mimi — ingredient bootstrap checklist

**For the household to mark up. Drafted 2026-08-23 (M9/WP3.3).**

This is the one-time list that teaches Mimi what **not** to cook. She has no memory of past meals and no way to guess — so anything left unmarked here, she will treat as fair game.

⚠️ **It is deliberately short.** A long questionnaire does not get filled in, and an unfilled questionnaire teaches her nothing. Skim each table, mark only what you actually feel strongly about, and leave the rest blank. **Blank is a valid and expected answer.**

## How to mark this

Put a letter in each person's column. Only two marks exist:

| Mark | Means | What Mimi does |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **N** | **hard-never** | ⛔ Never plans a dish containing it for that person. Absolute. |
| **a** | **soft-avoid** | Avoids it when there's a reasonable alternative; may still suggest it occasionally. |
| *(blank)* | no strong feeling | Treated as fine to cook. |

**One mark per cell.** If a dish is fine but you'd rather not eat it weekly, that's **a**, not **N**. Reserve **N** for genuine won't-eat-it / can't-eat-it — allergies, and the things that would make someone skip the meal entirely.

⚠️ **`N` and `a` mean different things and are not degrees of the same thing.** A hard-never removes a dish from the plan; a soft-avoid only nudges the ranking. Marking everything **N** would leave Mimi almost nothing to cook.

# tri-state exit to one bit, mapping "the probe FAILED TO RUN" (rc ≥ 2: bad regex,

# PROBE-ERRORS; six assertions greened in one sitting off an unset $GREP). This helper

# anything else = PROBE ERROR = FAIL loudly, naming the rc.

# died inside an earlier $(...)) still reads as "absent." This closes the grep-level
# error class, not the empty-input class — pair with a non-emptiness assertion where
# the input's existence is itself in question.
refute_grep() {

# --- M9/WP3: Mimi's store schema and conventions -----------------------------------
#
# WHAT THIS SECTION PROTECTS, AND WHY EACH ASSERTION EXISTS
#
# The store is RUNTIME STATE on the box, so most of these are LIVE. The one hermetic
# assertion covers the repo-side artifact (the returned bootstrap checklist), because
# 01_Preferences.md is transcribed FROM it and a lost original makes the transcription
# unverifiable.
#
# The store's central defect class is an AUTHORED INSTRUCTION CONTRADICTING THE REAL
# SHAPE OF THE DATA. Noey's store produced it three times, and the wrong-order variant
# twice, because the ordering convention was only ever INFERRED from the data and never
# written down. ⛔ A file with the right content in the WRONG ORDER is still a valid
# file: it passes bash -n, md5, YAML parsing, and every verify-self subagent. The only
# mechanical defence is to require each file to DECLARE its own convention, and that is
# what the loop below asserts — over a DERIVED set, with seen == expected, so adding a
# store file cannot silently un-cover the existing ones.

printf '\n[hermetic] M9/WP3 — the returned bootstrap checklist survives in the repo\n'

# The RETURNED checklist is the evidence for every entry in 01_Preferences.md. It is
# repo-side (docs/ is NOT a deploy payload), so it is assertable hermetically.
wp3_ret='docs/mimi-ingredient-bootstrap-checklist-RETURNED-2026-08-24.md'

# CONTROL FIRST: the file must be non-empty. ⛔ Do NOT use `grep -qv` for this — it
# returns rc 1 on an EMPTY file, so an empty input and a fully-matching one are
# indistinguishable, which is the exact dead-instrument case a control exists to exclude
# (CLAUDE.md, M5/WP5b). Use -s for existence+size, then a POSITIVE grep for content.
check "$([[ -s "$wp3_ret" ]] && echo 0 || echo 1)" \
      "the returned bootstrap checklist exists and is non-empty" \
      "$wp3_ret is missing or empty" \
      "01_Preferences.md is transcribed FROM this file; without it the transcription cannot be re-verified"

if [[ -s "$wp3_ret" ]]; then
  # POSITIVE control: the marking vocabulary must be present. If this fails, the file
  # exists but is not the marked instrument, and the count below would measure nothing.
  /usr/bin/grep -q 'hard-never' "$wp3_ret"
  check "$?" "the returned checklist carries the two-tier vocabulary" \
        "the returned checklist does not mention 'hard-never'" \
        "the file is present but is not the marked instrument — a count over it would measure nothing"

  # The household actually marked it. A returned-but-blank checklist is the failure mode
  # that would seed an EMPTY 01_Preferences.md while looking like a completed round-trip.
  # 39 cells were marked on 2026-08-24; assert a floor, not the exact number, so ordinary
  # later edits do not fail the suite.
  wp3_marks="$(/usr/bin/grep -cE '^\|[^|]*\|[[:space:]]*(\*\*)?[Na]' "$wp3_ret" || true)"
  check "$([[ "$wp3_marks" -ge 10 ]] && echo 0 || echo 1)" \
        "the returned checklist is actually marked ($wp3_marks marked rows)" \
        "the returned checklist has almost no markings ($wp3_marks)" \
        "a blank return would seed an EMPTY preferences file while looking like a completed round-trip"
fi

if [[ $HERMETIC_ONLY -eq 1 ]]; then
  skip "M9/WP3 store invariants" "--hermetic requested"
elif ! instance_up; then
  skip "M9/WP3 store invariants" "instance unreachable"
else
  printf '\n[live] M9/WP3 — Mimi store conventions and the derived index\n'

  wp3_store='/home/ubuntu/mimi-store'
  wp3_present="$(ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
    "test -d $wp3_store && echo yes || echo no" 2>/dev/null || echo no)"

  if [[ "$wp3_present" != "yes" ]]; then
    # NOT a pass and NOT silent — name the gap. ⚠️ Mimi's terminal.cwd points here, and
    # the gateway reports active even when it does not exist (measured 2026-08-23), so
    # absence is a real state that no health signal reveals.
    skip "M9/WP3 store invariants" \
         "$wp3_store does not exist — nothing to assert. ⚠️ This is NOT benign: Mimi's terminal.cwd points at it and the gateway still reports active"
  else
    # DERIVE the subject set from the box. ⛔ Never hand-enumerate the file list: a store
    # file added later must be covered the moment it appears, with no maintenance here.
    wp3_files="$(ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
      "find $wp3_store -maxdepth 1 -name '*.md' | sort" 2>/dev/null || true)"
    wp3_expected="$(printf '%s' "$wp3_files" | /usr/bin/grep -c . || true)"

    # CONTROL: the derivation found something. A zero here would make every loop below
    # vacuously pass — "nothing found" is indistinguishable from "nothing to find"
    # unless the count is asserted (CLAUDE.md: reads of ABSENCE).
    check "$([[ "$wp3_expected" -ge 6 ]] && echo 0 || echo 1)" \
          "the store's file set derives non-trivially ($wp3_expected top-level .md files)" \
          "derived only $wp3_expected store files — the loops below would pass vacuously" \
          "a search returning (almost) nothing is indistinguishable from a subject with nothing to find"

    # INVARIANT 1 — every store file DECLARES its ordering convention.
    # ⚠️ seen == expected, NOT -ge 1. A `head -1`-shaped or existence-shaped check is
    # coverage that SHRINKS as the set grows: adding a file would silently un-cover the
    # others while the assertion total never moves (CLAUDE.md, M9/WP2).
    wp3_seen=0; wp3_missing=""
    while IFS= read -r f; do
      [[ -n "$f" ]] || continue
      if ssh -n -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
           "grep -q '^\*\*Ordering:\*\*' '$f'" 2>/dev/null; then
        wp3_seen=$(( wp3_seen + 1 ))
      else
        wp3_missing="${wp3_missing} $(basename "$f")"
      fi
    done <<< "$wp3_files"
    # ⚠️ `ssh -n` is REQUIRED in this loop: without it ssh drains the loop's stdin and the
    # loop iterates ONCE, which reads as a pass on a one-element set (measured M9/WP2).
    check "$([[ "$wp3_seen" -eq "$wp3_expected" ]] && echo 0 || echo 1)" \
          "every store file declares its own ordering convention ($wp3_seen/$wp3_expected)" \
          "store files without a declared ordering convention:${wp3_missing:- none} ($wp3_seen/$wp3_expected)" \
          "Noey's store cost the SAME wrong-order defect twice because the convention was inferred from the data, never written down — and a right-content-wrong-order file passes every other check"

    # INVARIANT 2 — the cooked log states NEWEST-FIRST specifically.
    # The generic convention check above cannot see WHICH order a file declares, and this
    # is the exact file whose order was got wrong twice on Noey.
    ssh -n -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
      "grep -qi 'REVERSE CHRONOLOGICAL' $wp3_store/05_Cooked_Log.md" 2>/dev/null
    check "$?" "05_Cooked_Log.md declares reverse-chronological (newest first)" \
          "05_Cooked_Log.md does not declare newest-first ordering" \
          "entries PREPEND here; the append/prepend confusion is Noey's twice-repeated defect"

    # INVARIANT 3 — D21 lives on the INVENTORY, never on a recipe.
    # ⚠️ This is a read of ABSENCE, so it needs its positive control: prove the pattern
    # matches a case known to be present before believing emptiness (CLAUDE.md).
    wp3_ctl="$(ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
      "grep -rl 'Acquired' $wp3_store/03_Inventory.md 2>/dev/null | wc -l" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)"
    check "$([[ "$wp3_ctl" -ge 1 ]] && echo 0 || echo 1)" \
          "CONTROL: the shelf-life vocabulary IS present where it belongs (03_Inventory.md)" \
          "'Acquired' not found in 03_Inventory.md — the absence check below would say nothing" \
          "a pattern that matches nothing anywhere cannot distinguish 'absent' from 'broken probe'"

    wp3_leak="$(ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
      "grep -rl 'shelf_life\|perishable_driver' $wp3_store/recipes/ 2>/dev/null | wc -l" 2>/dev/null || echo 0)"
    check "$([[ "$wp3_leak" -eq 0 ]] && echo 0 || echo 1)" \
          "no recipe carries a shelf-life key (D21 is per-item INVENTORY state)" \
          "$wp3_leak recipe(s) carry a shelf-life field" \
          "arch.md D21: perishability is a property of the ITEM in the fridge with a clock already running, NEVER of a dish — a recipe field cannot express that THIS vegetable is 6 days old, cannot see an item no dish uses, and cannot say 'throw it away'"

    # INVARIANT 4 — the index is DERIVED. Rebuild into a temp copy and diff.
    # ⛔ The generator writes in place, so it is run against a COPY of the store's recipe
    # set rather than mutating the live index during a test run.
    wp3_diff="$(ssh -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
      "set -e
       t=\$(mktemp -d); mkdir -p \$t/recipes
       cp $wp3_store/recipes/*.md \$t/recipes/ 2>/dev/null
       cp $wp3_store/build-index.py \$t/ 2>/dev/null
       cd \$t && python3 build-index.py \$t >/dev/null 2>&1
       if diff -q \$t/00_Recipe_Index.md $wp3_store/00_Recipe_Index.md >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo same; else echo differ; fi
       rm -rf \$t" 2>/dev/null || echo error)"
    check "$([[ "$wp3_diff" == "same" ]] && echo 0 || echo 1)" \
          "00_Recipe_Index.md is exactly reproducible from recipes/*.md (arch.md D15)" \
          "the index does not regenerate identically (got: $wp3_diff)" \
          "D15: the index is STRICTLY derived and planning reads only it — a drifted index means planning sees something the recipes do not say. On disagreement the recipe files win; rerun build-index.py"

    # INVARIANT 5 — the index carries the D20 fields.
    # ⚠️ planning reads ONLY the index, so a thaw requirement absent from it is invisible
    # at exactly the moment it matters, and the dish becomes uncookable rather than worse.
    ssh -n -o ConnectTimeout=10 -o BatchMode=yes hermes \
      "grep -qi 'thaw' $wp3_store/00_Recipe_Index.md" 2>/dev/null
    check "$?" "the derived index carries the D20 thaw column" \
          "the index has no thaw column" \
          "plan-week reads ONLY the index (D15); a thaw requirement missing here is invisible at planning time and the dish becomes UNCOOKABLE, not merely worse"
  fi
fi

cd /Users/stayman/Personal/projects/my-hermes-agent
cat >> docs/lessons/guard-discipline.md <<'EOF'

---

## A word is not a structure — anchoring, and the two ways the repair nearly failed

**Measured 2026-08-24 (M9/WP3), on my own new assertions.**

Five live invariants were written for Mimi's store. Four were injection-proven and fired correctly. The
fifth — *"the derived index carries D20's thaw column"* — was written as:

```sh
grep -qi 'thaw' 00_Recipe_Index.md
```

Renaming the **column** `Thaw` → `Tx` left it **GREEN**. The index's own explanatory prose says "thaw"
**six times** (*"a thaw requirement missing here is invisible at planning time"*, *"frozen protein cannot be
thawed at 6:05am"*, …), so the word survives the column's deletion intact.

⛔ **The assertion measured the documentation, not the schema.** And the documentation is the part *least*
likely to change when someone breaks the schema — so the guard was anti-correlated with the thing it
protected.

📌 **THE RULE: when asserting that a STRUCTURE exists, anchor to the structure.** Match the table header row,
the key line, the declaration — not a word that also appears in prose about it. A bare word cannot
distinguish *"the column exists"* from *"the file talks about the column."*

### The sibling that was blind only by luck

The neighbouring invariant (`grep -qi 'REVERSE CHRONOLOGICAL'` on the cooked-log) had the **identical
shape**. It happened to pass a real injection — because that phrase occurs exactly once in that file today.
⚠️ **That is luck, not construction.** An injection proved the difference on a real case:

| Injection | bare-word form | anchored form |
|---|---|---|
| Flip the `**Ordering:**` declaration | fires | fires |
| Flip the declaration **and** add the phrase to prose | ⛔ **stays GREEN** | fires |

The second row is the realistic failure: prose accumulates, and the guard silently weakens to *"the file
mentions the concept"* while the declaration it exists to pin can be changed freely.

### Two ways the REPAIR nearly failed, both cheap to avoid

1. **My first replacement pattern matched 0 on the real header.** ⚠️ A guard that fires at baseline is the
   tell that the *pattern* is wrong, not the subject. The culprit was `*` quantifiers around the spaces
   (`\| *Thaw *\|` against `.*\|` greediness). 📌 **Build the pattern up incrementally against the real line**
   — anchor only, then one column, then both — instead of guessing a second complete regex.

2. **My test OF the test was wrong.** I wrote
   `r=$(ssh … "grep -c …" || echo 0)` and compared `[ "$r" = "0" ]`. On a firing assertion the capture was
   `"0\n0"` — grep's own `0` plus the fallback's — so the comparison was **false on a value that was zero**,
   and the harness printed **"STILL BLIND: FAIL"** for an assertion that had actually fired correctly.
   📌 **Key the test-of-the-test on the EXIT CODE the suite itself uses** (`grep -q`), never on captured
   output. ⚠️ This is the instrument-over-artifact pattern one level up: a broken *verifier of a verifier*,
   reporting a false red. Had I believed it, I would have "fixed" a working guard.

⚠️ **Distinct from *assert on proximity, not presence*** (above). That rule governs a **qualifier near a
claim** — a count cannot express "this statement is qualified." This one governs a **word standing in for a
structure**, where the word is present in prose whether or not the structure survives.
EOF
echo "lesson appended"; wc -l docs/lessons/guard-discipline.md

# Feature Verify — Automated

You are an expert QA Engineer running fast, scoped automated checks immediately after a build step.

## State Machine Context

You are in the **feature** workflow at the **verify-auto** state.
This is the first step of the per-phase verification loop: `build → verify-auto → verify-self → verify-human → verify-codify`.

**Valid transitions from here:**
- **F10 → verify-self:** Tests pass → tell user to run `/feature-verify-self <dev-url>`
- **F9 → build (back-loop):** Tests fail → document failures, tell user to run `/feature-build` to fix
- **F24 → spec (back-loop):** Tests reveal the spec was wrong → document what's wrong, tell user to run `/feature-spec`

## Orchestrator Pause Policy (cheat-sheet)

When invoked by `/session-start` in orchestrated mode, the orchestrator reads `TRANSITION: <id>` and uses this table to decide whether to chain or pause. Per-skill rows for verify-auto's exits:

| Transition | Mode 1 — Stepping | Mode 2 — Orchestrated | Mode 3 — Autopilot | Mode 4 — FSD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F10 (verify-auto → verify-self) | PAUSE | AUTO | AUTO | AUTO |
| F9 (back-loop to build) | PAUSE | AUTO | AUTO | AUTO |
| F24 (back-loop to spec) | PAUSE | AUTO | AUTO | AUTO |

**Hard rule for AUTO exits.** When this skill's emitted transition is `AUTO` in the current drive mode, the orchestrator **must immediately invoke the next skill via the `Skill` tool**. It must **NOT** return control to the user. Emitting a clean `TRANSITION: F10` followed by a polite narrative summary ("Tests pass; ready to run verify-self") is the regression mode this block exists to prevent (P1 incident, 2026-05-16): the `TRANSITION` token is the chain signal; the summary text is not a stop signal. If the transition you just emitted is AUTO in the active drive mode, your next action is a `Skill` invocation, not a turn-end. **This explicitly includes the `AskUserQuestion` tool (and any other user-input/confirmation prompt): invoking it on an AUTO transition IS "returning control to the user" and is the same regression class as the narrative-summary stop above — do NOT call it to "just confirm" the handoff. The only thing that pauses an AUTO transition is the human-input points the active drive mode's pause policy explicitly marks PAUSE.** See `agents/feature-workflow/AGENTS.md` → "Pause policy by drive mode" for the canonical table and the precedence rule.

## Role and Scope

**verify-auto is a cheap, fast, early-indicator check — not a full QA pass.**

Its job is to catch obvious breakage in the specific code that was just changed: syntax errors, import failures, type errors, and basic smoke behaviour. The checks are temporary and one-off; they may or may not be codified into permanent tests later (that happens in verify-codify).

**Do NOT run the full test suite here.** Running the full suite is slow, catches regressions that belong to other phases, and blurs the signal. verify-auto must be scoped to the change just made.

Concrete examples of appropriate verify-auto checks:
- **Syntax / parse:** `python -m py_compile mymodule.py` or `node --check myfile.js`
- **Lint:** `ruff check mymodule.py` or `eslint src/mycomponent.tsx`
- **Import smoke:** `python -c "from mymodule import MyClass; MyClass()"` — confirms the module loads and the class is instantiable
- **Type check (scoped):** `mypy mymodule.py` or `tsc --noEmit src/mycomponent.tsx`
- **Unit smoke:** run a single targeted test file, not the full suite — e.g. `pytest tests/test_mymodule.py`

## Procedure

### 1. Identify What to Verify
- Read the WIP plan in `workflow-system/state/wip/`
- Identify the specific files changed in this build step
- Select 2–4 cheap checks scoped to those files only

### 2. Run Scoped Checks

**All tests pass (F10):**
- Update WIP tree: mark `verify-auto` node `[x]`, update `## Current Node`
- Tell user to run `/feature-verify-self <dev-url>` for live-system self-verification (user must supply the URL)

**Tests fail (F9):**

  - **Spec problem:** If the tests reveal the spec itself was wrong (not just the code), document the discrepancy and tell user to run `/feature-spec` (F24)

### 4. Report
Present a clear summary:
- Tests run / passed / failed
- Any warnings from linters or static analysis
- Recommendation for next step

### 5. Emit Transition
End your output with the canonical transition token so the orchestrator can act on it (the orchestrator reads `TRANSITION: <id>`; the bare slash-command prose above is advisory for single-step users only):

- `TRANSITION: F10` — tests pass, hand off to verify-self

Base directory for this skill: /Users/stayman/.claude/skills/feature-verify-self

# Feature Verify — Self (Agent)

You are an expert QA Engineer running live-system self-verification before handing off to a human.

## State Machine Context

You are in the **feature** workflow at the **verify-self** state.
This is the second step of the per-phase verification loop: `build → verify-auto → verify-self → verify-human → verify-codify`.

**Valid transitions from here:**
- **F10b → verify-human:** All blocking issues resolved (or none found) → tell user to run `/feature-verify-human`
- **F9b → build (back-loop):** Blocking issue found that agent can fix → document it, tell user to run `/feature-build`

## Orchestrator Pause Policy (cheat-sheet)

When invoked by `/session-start` in orchestrated mode, the orchestrator reads `TRANSITION: <id>` and uses this table to decide whether to chain or pause. Per-skill rows for verify-self's exits:

| Transition | Mode 1 — Stepping | Mode 2 — Orchestrated | Mode 3 — Autopilot | Mode 4 — FSD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F10b (verify-self → verify-human) | PAUSE | AUTO (chain into verify-human, which itself PAUSEs) | AUTO (chain into verify-human, which itself PAUSEs) | AUTO — **skip verify-human entirely**, chain directly to `feature-verify-codify` |
| F9b (back-loop to build) | PAUSE | AUTO | AUTO | AUTO |

**Hard rule for AUTO exits.** When this skill's emitted transition is `AUTO` in the current drive mode, the orchestrator **must immediately invoke the next skill via the `Skill` tool**. It must **NOT** return control to the user. Emitting a clean `TRANSITION: F10b` followed by a polite narrative summary ("Verify-self complete; ready to run verify-human") is the regression mode this block exists to prevent (P1 incident, 2026-05-16): the `TRANSITION` token is the chain signal; the summary text is not a stop signal. If the transition you just emitted is AUTO in the active drive mode, your next action is a `Skill` invocation, not a turn-end. **This explicitly includes the `AskUserQuestion` tool (and any other user-input/confirmation prompt): invoking it on an AUTO transition IS "returning control to the user" and is the same regression class as the narrative-summary stop above — do NOT call it to "just confirm" the handoff. The only thing that pauses an AUTO transition is the human-input points the active drive mode's pause policy explicitly marks PAUSE.** See `agents/feature-workflow/AGENTS.md` → "Pause policy by drive mode" for the canonical table and the precedence rule.

## Severity Taxonomy

Use this taxonomy consistently when classifying failures. It is also embedded in the subagent prompt.

| Severity | Definition | Examples |
|----------|-----------|---------|
| **BLOCKING** | The feature cannot be considered working. A human handed this would immediately reject it. | Blank page or white screen; JS console error on load; application crash; missing required element (form field, button, nav link); broken navigation (404, redirect loop); auth failure (can't log in); data loss (save doesn't persist); wrong HTTP status on a critical endpoint (500 instead of 200, 404 on existing resource) |
| **COSMETIC** | The feature works but has a visual or copy imperfection. A human might note it but would not reject the phase. | Spacing or padding off; wrong color or font; copy typo or wrong label text; minor layout deviation from design; non-critical missing decoration (icon, border radius) |

**Decision rule:** When in doubt, classify as BLOCKING. A false BLOCKING sends you to fix something minor; a false COSMETIC ships a broken feature to the human.

## Subagent Re-Verification Heuristic

**Rule:** If N-1 of N outcomes PASS and the Nth FAIL is mechanically implied by the PASSes, suspect snapshot timing before back-looping; re-run the same Playwright assertions directly from the orchestrator before invoking `/feature-build` with scoped leaves.

**Why this exists:** Verify-self subagents observe the page through Playwright snapshots. On pages whose interactive surface is JIT-compiled in the browser (Babel-standalone in-page transformation), lazily mounted (React lazy / async chunks), or hydrated after an async data fetch, the subagent's snapshot can be taken *before* the relevant DOM/handlers exist. The subagent then reports a BLOCKING FAIL on an outcome that — at observation time — was genuinely not satisfiable, but which the page **does** satisfy a few hundred milliseconds later. Back-looping to build at that point sends the next phase to fix a non-bug.

**Trigger pattern (all conditions must hold):**

1. The subagent reported at least one PASS in the same run.
2. The reported FAIL is **mechanically implied** by the PASSes — i.e., the failing outcome cannot be false if the passing outcomes are true. ("The hash-restore PASS asserts viewport=720:780, which mechanically implies the ticks PASS that just FAILed must also be true.") This is the calibration that separates genuine fails from snapshot-timing noise.
3. The page under test uses an in-browser JIT pipeline, lazy mount, or pre-render async fetch.

If any one of these does not hold, treat the FAIL as genuine and back-loop normally.

**Procedure when the heuristic fires:**

1. Do **not** mark the failed leaf `FAILED` yet. Do not emit `TRANSITION: F9b`.
2. Re-run the failing outcome's assertions **directly from the orchestrator** (not via a fresh subagent) using the same Playwright MCP tools the subagent used. Wait for the interactive surface to be ready before asserting (`browser_wait_for` on a known late-mounting selector, or `browser_evaluate` to poll for the relevant `window.*` value before snapshotting).
3. Common workaround for React-controlled UI: synthetic DOM events (clicks dispatched via `browser_click` on stale snapshots, `WheelEvent` dispatched via `browser_evaluate`) often do not reach React's synthetic event system on a JIT page. Direct invocation via the React fiber works reliably: `browser_evaluate` something like `el[Object.keys(el).find(k => k.startsWith('__reactProps'))].onClick()` (or equivalent for `onChange`, `onWheel`, etc.). This pattern has been the consistent fix across multiple instances of this heuristic firing.
4. If the direct re-verification **PASSes**: the original FAIL was a snapshot-timing artifact. Mark the leaf `[x]`, document the re-verification in the WIP file (one line: "Re-verified directly; subagent's FAIL was snapshot-timing noise — orchestrator confirmed PASS."), and proceed to F10b.
5. If the direct re-verification **FAILs** the same way: the FAIL is genuine. Mark the leaf `FAILED`, document the orchestrator-side re-verification result, and back-loop F9b normally.

**What this heuristic is not:** It is not license to override subagent findings whenever a FAIL is inconvenient. The mechanical-implication test is the gate — if you cannot state in one sentence why the PASSes imply the FAIL must also be true, the FAIL is genuine and back-loop is the right path.

## Integration-boundary rule

A phase has an **integration boundary** when any of the following is true of the implementation leaves under the current phase:

1. A line of code was added or modified inside a file that an existing HTTP endpoint, route, controller, GraphQL resolver, RPC handler, or middleware already consumed.
2. A line of code was added or modified inside a file that backs an existing UI page, view, or component such that user-visible behavior changes.
3. A line of code was added or modified inside an existing CLI command, subcommand, or argument parser.
4. A line of code was added or modified inside an existing scheduled job, cron, queue consumer, or background worker.
5. The request/response shape, payload, or destination of an existing outbound call to an external system was changed.

If a boundary applies, **at least one Observable Outcome for this phase must cite the consuming surface by name** — the existing endpoint path, route URL, UI page URL, CLI command, job name, or external-call target. An outcome that only exercises the new module or new dedicated admin/status endpoints does not satisfy this rule.

If you reach §1 of the procedure and find the current phase has a boundary but no outcome citing the consuming surface, **do not run the verification subagent**. Instead, document the missing outcome and back-loop to build (F9b) so the plan can be updated and the missing outcome verified. Cite the specific consuming surface (e.g. `POST /distribution/match`) in your back-loop message.

If a boundary does not apply (the phase only adds isolated new artifacts — a new module nothing imports, a new endpoint nothing links to, a constant, a renamed private function), this rule does not apply. Note in your output: "No integration boundary — phase adds isolated new artifacts only."

**The spawn is unconditional.** Per `workflow-system/product/arch.md` (Revision 2026-04-27, "verify-self runs as a subagent"), the verification work runs in a one-shot subagent so that Playwright snapshots, console-message dumps, and accessibility-tree output stay in the subagent's context — *parent context stays lean across multi-phase features*. The spawn fires regardless of whether the phase's Observable Outcomes happen to need Playwright; the design property is parent-context cleanliness, not tool availability. Do not skip the spawn because outcomes "look CLI-verifiable." The subagent's agent definition at `agents/feature-verify-self-runner/AGENTS.md` carries the job description, severity taxonomy, and procedure — you provide only the dynamic context.

**Assemble the dynamic context:**

1. `<dev-url>` — from `{{args}}` (the URL the running app is at).
2. `<observable-outcomes>` — verbatim from the current phase's `**Observable outcomes:**` block in the WIP tree.

```
Observable outcomes to verify:
```

#### In-place fix shortcut (BLOCKING-fail handling — narrow exception)

verify-self is contractually observe-only: BLOCKING failures normally route through the F9b back-loop to `feature-build`. This sub-clause defines a narrow exception that permits an in-place fix when the back-loop would cost 3 extra Skill invocations (build → verify-auto → verify-self) for an outcome equivalent to what the back-loop itself would have produced.

**All three gates must hold:**

1. **Trivial extension of the just-completed leaf.** The fix is a one-line (or small, mechanical) extension of code/config/test scaffolding written in the just-completed impl leaf. It is *not* a redesign, a re-plan, a new abstraction, or a fix that crosses files/modules outside the leaf's scope. If you cannot describe the fix in one sentence as "extend X that was just written in P<N>.<M>", the gate fails — use F9b instead.
2. **Fresh model invocation re-verifies.** Re-verification of the fixed leaf goes through a fresh model invocation — either a freshly-spawned Playwright subagent (preferred, identical artifact to what F9b → verify-self would produce), or a fresh `Skill` invocation of `feature-verify-self` against the same Observable Outcome. Re-verification by the same agent re-reading its own state does NOT count and does NOT satisfy this gate.
3. **Audit-trail entry in WIP `## Discoveries`.** Append an entry of the form `[SHORTCUT-<YYYY-MM-DD>] <leaf-id> — <one-line description of what was fixed and how it was re-verified>` to the WIP file's `## Discoveries` section before transitioning. The entry is the artifact a reviewer can grep for when reconstructing why the F9b back-loop was bypassed.

Rule of three observed instances codified 2026-06-09: v3 WP3 Phase 2 (2026-05-29), v3 WP11 Phase 1 (2026-06-06), verify-human-auto-skip-when-no-integration-boundary Phase 2 (2026-06-07). All three were ad-hoc deviations user-approved at verify-human; this clause formalizes them.
